title: The Southern Taurids Are Here — Watch for Fireballs!
summary:
Have you ever seen a shooting star? Right now, one of the longest meteor showers of the year is happening — and it might show you something amazing. The Southern Taurids began on Sept. 20 and run until Nov. 20.

This shower isn't about quantity. You'll only see about five to 10 meteors per hour at its peak. But the Taurids are famous for fireballs — super bright meteors that flash across the sky. They also move slowly, around 17 miles per second, so you can watch them longer than most meteors. Some leave glowing trails behind them.

The best nights to watch are Oct. 13-14 and Nov. 4-5. On Oct. 13-14, the sky will be moonless and dark — perfect for stargazing. On Nov. 4-5, a thin crescent moon rises early in the morning, so it won't block much light.

Where do they come from? The meteors are tiny pieces of rock left behind by Comet 2P/Encke. Earth passes through this debris trail every year.

You don't need binoculars or a telescope — just your eyes and a wide view of the sky. Meteors can appear anywhere overhead, so lie back, be patient, and enjoy the show.
why_it_matters: Knowing when meteor showers happen lets families plan a free, easy night of sky-watching together — no special equipment, just a dark spot and some patience.

background_read: A meteor shower happens when Earth travels through a trail of dust and tiny rocks left behind by a comet, and those bits burn up in our sky as shooting stars.
The Taurids are named after Taurus (a group of stars shaped like a bull) because the meteors seem to come from that part of the sky.
The comet that made this trail, Comet 2P/Encke, is named after the astronomer who figured out its path around the Sun — it swings past Earth again and again on a regular schedule.
